n: In this topic we study firearm injuries. In a firearm, the injuring projectile is set in motion by the energy of powder gases, and an injury inflicted by such a weapon is called a firearm injury. Injuries from the explosion of an artillery shell, mine, grenade and various explosive substances are also included. In forensic medical practice, such injuries are less common than mechanical injuries from blunt and sharp objects. Nevertheless, law enforcement agencies pay special attention to these incidents and carry out a thorough investigation.

What is distinctive about firearm injuries? Unlike blunt and sharp objects, they are linked to the design features of weapons and ammunition. The projectile has a relatively small mass but a high velocity and can inflict injury from a long distance. Not only mechanical but also thermal, chemical and other kinds of action are involved. In forensic medicine these injuries are conventionally divided into two groups: injuries from firearms and blast trauma.

Firearms are classified by several features. By purpose, there are military, hunting, sporting, gas and special weapons. By manufacture, a typical weapon is made in specialised production, while an atypical weapon is home-made or modified. By manner of use, firearms are individual, that is, rifle, assault rifle, pistol, or crew-served, that is, machine gun. By barrel length, long weapons are distinguished, that is, rifles and carbines, medium weapons, that is, submachine guns, and short weapons, that is, pistols and revolvers.

Now the barrel, rifling and calibre. A rifled barrel has 4-6 helical grooves. They impart a rotating motion to the bullet, so the bullet flies farther and more accurately. In a rifled barrel, the calibre is measured in millimetres by the distance between opposite lands. In a smooth-bore barrel the inner surface is smooth, and the calibre is given by the number of lead balls to the pound; such a barrel is used in hunting weapons for shot. Attention: in a smooth-bore barrel, the larger the calibre number, the smaller the diameter of the bore. A rifled barrel is characteristic of military and sporting weapons.

Sporting weapons hardly differ in construction from military ones. Their barrel is usually small-calibre, 5.6 mm, and rifled. Hunting weapons have a smooth-bore or rifled barrel. The smooth-bore type is intended for shot, with a calibre of 10-32; the 12 and 16 gauges are more common. Special weapons also use the energy of powder gases: starting, signal and construction-assembly pistols belong here. By manner of loading, automatic and non-automatic weapons are distinguished. In automatic weapons, loading is carried out by powder gases.

t: Quick question: types of weapon and calibre
n: Quick questions. First question: what is the difference between a typical and an atypical weapon? An atypical weapon is home-made or modified, for example a rifle with a shortened barrel and stock. Second question: what is rifling for? It imparts a rotating motion to the projectile, so the bullet flies faster, farther and more accurately. Third question: what are the calibre categories? Small calibre up to 6 mm, medium 7-9 mm, large 10 mm and above. Fourth question: how does the diameter change as the calibre number increases in a smooth-bore hunting weapon? Answer: it decreases.

Let us consider the structure of a military cartridge. In a unitary cartridge the bullet, that is, the projectile, the powder charge and the primer are placed in the cartridge case as a single whole. The projectile is made of steel or steel with a lead jacket, and the case of steel, brass or iron. The primer is located at the base of the case and has a brass cover; its composition includes lead styphnate, antimony and potassium chlorate. The powder is smokeless and is made of nitrocellulose. The tip of a bullet for a long-barrelled weapon is somewhat pointed, while for a short-barrelled weapon the tip is rounded or shaped like a truncated cone.

t: Special bullets and types of powder
n: Special bullets and types of powder. The core of an armour-piercing bullet is special steel; an incendiary bullet contains phosphorus, and a tracer barium and magnesium. An explosive bullet breaks into small pieces on hitting the target; international agreements prohibit it in combat. There are two kinds of powder. Smokeless powder, based on nitrocellulose, gives 3 times more gas than black powder; this increases bullet energy and range, and it is used in military and sporting weapons. Black powder consists of potassium nitrate, charcoal and sulphur, gives about 300 cubic cm of gas from 1 g, and is used in hunting weapons, signal pistols and gas weapons.

The structure of a shot cartridge consists of layers. The case is brass, plastic or cardboard, and black powder may be used as the charge. The order is as follows: case and primer, powder charge, cardboard and felt wads, pellets, then the wad closing the shot. Shot is pellets 1 to 5.5 mm in diameter; larger shot is called buckshot. A ball cartridge may contain a lead ball more than 10 mm in diameter, a Jakan or Brenneke bullet.

t: Case analysis: distinguishing weapon and cartridge type
n: Case analysis: distinguishing the type of weapon and cartridge. Situation: a short-barrelled weapon and several cartridge cases have been found at the scene. On the inner surface of the barrel there are 4-6 helical grooves. Barrel feature: rifling indicates a military or sporting weapon, while a smooth bore is more characteristic of hunting weapons firing shot. Cartridge feature: in a unitary cartridge the bullet, powder and primer are in the case, whereas a shot cartridge has wads and shot of 1-5.5 mm. Question: which features indicate the type of weapon and cartridge? Attention: a home-made or modified weapon is considered atypical.

Injuring factors of a shot. The primary projectile is the bullet, the shot and their parts. A secondary projectile is an obstacle in the line of flight, clothing and bone fragments; they too cause injury. Attention: a primary projectile is not the same as a secondary projectile. The factors are divided into four groups: the main projectile, additional factors, the firearm and secondary projectiles. Additional factors include the air ahead of the muzzle, flame, gases, soot and powder. The weapon factor includes parts of the barrel formed when the barrel bursts.

Powder-gas pressure and projectile velocity. When powder burns, gases form within 0.01-0.001 sec. and great pressure arises in the cartridge chamber. In a smooth-bore barrel the pressure is 400-700 atm., in a rifled barrel 2000-3000 atm. Gas pressure acts on all sides of the barrel wall, and the weapon moves slightly backwards. In a smooth-bore barrel the projectile velocity is up to 500 m/sec; for a Makarov bullet 315 m/sec, for an AKM bullet 710 m/sec. The projectile rotates about its own axis up to 3000 times per second.

t: Additional factors and ranges of action
n: Additional factors and ranges of action. Additional factors include the air ahead of the muzzle, the flame of the shot, powder gases, soot, particles and oil droplets. The air ahead of the muzzle shows mechanical action at a distance of 3-5 cm, powder gases at 10-15 cm; the flame gives thermal action at 3-10 cm. The action depends on the construction of the weapon and cartridge, on previous shots, on the obstacle and on the injured surface. Under the pressure of powder gases the weapon moves backwards; in a home-made weapon the barrel may burst and the person holding the weapon may be injured.

Mechanical action is divided into three types: bursting, tearing-out and wedging. The type of action depends on the magnitude of the bullet's energy at the moment of hitting the target. In bursting action the energy is several thousand joules, the wound is large, the edges uneven, and there are radial tears. In tearing-out the energy is several hundred joules, the defect is smaller than the bullet, and the edges are smooth. In wedging action the energy is several tens of joules, and the wound is slit-like or stellate, without a defect. Pirogov described the tissue defect in 1849 and called it "loss of tissue's own substance". Attention: in tearing-out action there is a tissue defect, in wedging action there is not; the exit wound is usually of the wedging type.

Thermal action arises mainly from the flame of the shot and powder gases. The flame arises from the explosion of unburnt powder particles with atmospheric oxygen and acts at a distance of 3-10 cm. The flame and gases scorch clothing, skin and hair; secondary ignition of clothing also causes thermal injury. Soot, powder and metal particles cause superficial thermal injury. In chemical action, carboxyhaemoglobin forms in the blood and carboxymyoglobin in the muscle, and the area turns pink.

Chemical action comes from the powder gases: around the entrance wound, carboxyhaemoglobin forms in the blood and carboxymyoglobin in the muscles, and the area turns pink. Sometimes methaemoglobin and sulphaemoglobin also appear. Special bullets, that is, incendiary bullets or those containing a chemical substance, correspondingly produce thermal and chemical injury.

Case analysis: injuring factors. Situation: a burn, an abrasion and a pink tinge have been found around the wound. Question: which of the additional factors acted? Burn: the flame of the shot, 3-10 cm, and powder gases act thermally, scorching clothing, skin and hair. Abrasion: powder gases at a distance of 10-15 cm exert mechanical action, giving abrasion, bruising and tearing of soft tissue. Pink tinge: through the chemical action of powder gases, carboxyhaemoglobin forms in the blood and carboxymyoglobin in the muscle.

t: Range and distance of the shot
n: The range and the distance of the shot are not the same. Range is a certain set of signs, divided into contact, close and non-close; it is assessed by changes in the clothing and body. Distance, by contrast, is the interval between the muzzle of the barrel and the target, measured in units of length. Distance is determined only by experiment: test shots are fired from that weapon with that ammunition. Attention: the same range may correspond to a different distance with different weapons.

Injury in a contact shot. If powder gases reach the internal organs, the sharp expansion of gas causes extensive ruptures. The wound track contains soot and powder particles; its initial part is pink, because carboxyhaemoglobin forms. In a full contact shot, the entrance wound has a defect larger than the calibre, with detached and torn edges. Types of contact: fully hermetic, in which the gas presses the skin against the barrel and a stamp mark remains; full, in which the whole area of the muzzle is in contact; and oblique, in which the barrel is at an angle, a tear forms on one side and the soot looks "tongue-shaped".

At close range, three zones are distinguished according to the signs of additional factors. The length of a zone depends on the barrel length, calibre and construction of the cartridge. In the first zone there are signs of gas, soot, powder, metal and oil; for a Makarov about 1 cm, for an AK 3 cm, for a rifle 5 cm. In the second zone there is no sign of gas, while soot, powder and metal remain; in military weapons 25-35 cm. In the third zone only powder and metal particles remain; for a Makarov 150, for an AK 200, for a rifle 250 cm. With a hunting gun the third zone extends up to 500 cm.

t: Quick question: zones of close range
n: Quick questions: zones of close range. First question: in which zone are signs of the action of powder gases found? Answer: in the first zone. In the first zone the entrance wound arises from the tearing-out action of the bullet and the bursting, contusing action of the gas. Second question: in which zone are only powder and metal particles found among the additional factors? Answer: in the third zone. Third question: where do the additional factors remain if there is an obstacle between the barrel and the victim? Answer: on the obstacle; the bullet pierces the obstacle and hits the target.

t: Quick question: zones of close range (continued)
n: Fourth question: how does an obstacle affect the bullet? Answer: the bullet is deformed or breaks up, and its energy and direction may change. As a result an atypical injury is produced.

t: Non-close range and the Vinogradov phenomenon
n: At non-close range, there are no signs of additional factors on the clothing and around the entrance hole. Conditions of the Vinogradov phenomenon: velocity not less than 500 m/sec, clothing not tightly fitting and no strong wind. The mechanism is this: the bullet flies at high velocity, a low-pressure cavity forms behind it, soot enters this cavity and follows the bullet to the target, remaining on the inner layer or the body. The difference: at close range, soot is found outside the first layer, whereas here there is little soot, and it increases with distance from the edge.

Case analysis: determining the range. Situation: there is no soot on the outer layer of clothing, and a little soot on the inner layer. This is a sign not of close but of non-close range and of the Vinogradov phenomenon. Conditions: bullet velocity at impact not less than 500 m/sec; clothing not tightly fitting to the body or a space between the layers; no strong wind. Mechanism: behind a fast-flying bullet a low-pressure cavity forms, and soot enters it and reaches the target behind the bullet. Attention: at close range, soot is on the outer surface of the first layer; in the Vinogradov phenomenon, there is little soot, it lies far from the hole and increases towards the periphery.

t: Morphology of firearm injuries and impact theory
n: Morphology of firearm injuries and impact theory. The injury depends on the projectile: material, mass, calibre, length; on ballistics: velocity, precession, nutation, obstacles; and on the injured region: anatomical structure, density, volume, blood supply, and the presence of fluid and gas. The impact theory is as follows: a strong blow is delivered to a small surface, a wave spreads sideways from the track, phases of positive and negative pressure form, pulsation of a temporary cavity is observed, and particles of blood and tissue are expelled. The force of the blow spreads sideways and backwards too; the pulsation creates conditions for deeper penetration of the bullet.

t: Wound track and zones of the wound wall
n: By wound track, injuries are divided into several types. In a perforating wound there are entrance, track and exit. In a blind wound there is no exit, and the projectile remains at the end of the track. In a tangential wound the projectile does not enter fully, and an elongated abrasion or a groove-like wound forms. The track may be straight, broken or arc-shaped; there are continuous and discontinuous types. A discontinuous track arises from contraction of tissues and usually indicates that the injury was vital.

t: Wound track and zones of the wound wall (continued)
n: In the wound wall there are three zones: the track itself; the contusion zone, from 0.3 cm to 1-2 cm; and the concussion zone, 4-5 cm wide or more. A bullet whose centre of gravity has shifted downwards loses stability and transfers energy more fully to the tissues. As a result a large track, ruptures of internal organs and bone fractures are observed.

It is important to distinguish entrance and exit holes. At the entrance, at the wound edges there is an abrasion collar of 1-3 mm and above it a contamination collar; Pirogov described these collars in 1865 in his book "Principles of General Military Field Surgery". The entrance hole is round or oval, a tissue defect is often present, and the edges are smooth and turned inward. The exit hole is slit-like or stellate, a defect is rare, the edges are uneven and turned outward, and the collars are often absent. Attention: haemorrhage at the entrance is cuff-shaped, at the exit asymmetrical.

Firearm injury of bones. In a flat bone, a defect in the shape of a truncated cone forms at the site of entry; the projectile moves from the small base to the large one. In a tubular bone, on the entry side the defect is round with radial cracks, and on the exit side the defect is larger and the cracks run lengthwise. A defect is not characteristic of an exit hole. In thin regions such as the forearm and arm, if the bullet's energy is preserved, a defect may result from tearing-out action. Attention: in soft tissue, the defect at entry has the shape of a cone with its apex pointing inward, and at exit with its apex pointing outward.

t: Case analysis: entrance and exit holes
n: Case analysis: entrance and exit holes. Situation: the victim's forearm has two holes. In one, a tissue defect and an abrasion and contamination collar have been found; in the other, none. Question: which is the entrance hole? Justify the answer by the features: shape, edges, collars, haemorrhage. A defect, and an abrasion and contamination collar, are characteristic of an entrance. If skin folds form when the edges are brought together, a defect is present. Attention: the forearm is a thin region, so a defect may also be present at the exit. Rely not only on the defect but on the collars too.

Injury from a shot cartridge. A shot cartridge is used in smooth-bore hunting guns. Signs of powder and metal particles may be found up to 200-500 cm. Shot flies 200-400 m, large shot, that is, buckshot, up to 600 m; wads act up to 40 m. A shot cartridge usually produces blind wounds. The action varies with distance. In contact or up to 1 m the action is compact, a single hole equal to the diameter of the cartridge. Up to 5 m there is relative scatter: a main hole and small wounds around it. Beyond 5 m there is scatter: small wounds of similar shape and size.

Blank and pneumatic weapons. A blank cartridge contains no bullet: the injury arises from the action of powder gases in contact or at close distance. If fired in contact, the entrance hole has tears and a large defect; in the chest and abdomen, ruptures of internal organs are possible. The track is blind; with a carbine 10-15 cm, wads and fragments act for several metres. In a pneumatic weapon, compressed air operates, the pellet is deformed, and there are no signs of additional factors. If fired in contact, the air jet may leave a bruise. The injury is blind and does not pass through the body; the pellet reaches 30-50 m.

Injuries from gas weapons. A gas weapon may be barrelled or barrel-less, that is, a canister. The smooth bore has an obstruction inside. The calibre is most often 6, 8, 9 or 11.43 mm; in a 6 mm cartridge there is no powder. An irritant cartridge contains 20-1000 mg and acts at a distance of 2-3 m. The main effect lasts about an hour, and residual effects may be found for up to 7 days. Signs: pain, cough, lacrimation, blepharospasm. Complications: keratitis, conjunctivitis, tracheitis, bronchitis, pneumonia, skin wounds. For forensic chemical examination, small objects bearing traces of the irritant are taken; from skin and large objects, a gauze swab wash with ethyl alcohol is sent in a hermetic container.

In firearm injuries, 8 main questions are put to the examination; depending on the incident there may be additional ones. The sequence of questions: first whether it was fired from a weapon, then the type of weapon and projectile, then range and distance, entrance-exit and track, and finally the position of the barrel and of the victim. Firing from a weapon is established by the defect, the collars, signs of additional factors and the projectile in the body. Attention: range is a set of signs, while distance is the interval between barrel and target, determined by experiment.

t: Sequence of injuries and instrumental methods
n: Sequence of injuries and instrumental methods. In assessing sequence, in the first injury the haemorrhage is pronounced, soot and metal are more abundant in the next, while oil is more abundant in the first; a subsequent crack does not cross the earlier one. In an automatic weapon, the injuries are on one side, close together and of one kind. In a shot at oneself, the ability to press the trigger, the track, soot on the hand and traces of blood on the barrel are assessed. X-ray shows the bullet and shot, Bucky rays a metal particle, ultraviolet soot and oil, and infrared photography traces on dark clothing. The physician documents the entrance and exit holes and the track; the bullet, shot, clothing and footwear found are handed over in packaging to law enforcement.

Blast trauma. An explosion is the release of a large amount of energy in a short time; the types are natural, deliberate and accidental. Substances fall into three groups: primary, that is, initiating, secondary, that is, high explosive, and propellant, that is, powder. Types of action: mechanical, thermal, chemical and baroacoustic; in baroacoustic action the eardrum and lung are injured. An explosion has five factors: detonation products, the blast wave of the surrounding medium, fragments of the explosive device, special injuring means and secondary projectiles.

In an explosion, four ranges are conventionally distinguished: contact, close, relatively close and non-close. The distance corresponding to each range depends on the explosive, the device and the power of the charge. At contact range the main factors are detonation products and fragments. At close range, products, fragments and the blast wave. At relatively close range, the blast wave, fragments and secondary projectiles. At non-close range, fragments and secondary projectiles. In a device without a charge, in a cylinder the main factor is fragments of the wall, and in a steam boiler thermal injury.

Case analysis: explosion and examination. Situation: at the site of an explosion, foreign bodies have been found on the victim's body and clothing, and the eardrum is damaged. First question: from which factor is the injury to the eardrum and lung? Baroacoustic trauma comes mainly from the blast wave of the surrounding medium, sometimes from explosion gases. Second question: which range? The blast wave acts at close and relatively close range; additional information is needed for a precise answer. Third question: the physician fully examines and documents the bodily injuries and, as soon as possible, officially hands the foreign bodies to law enforcement.

Conclusion. Injuring factors: in a shot, the main projectile, additional factors, the weapon and secondary projectiles; in an explosion, five factors. Range is a set of signs and is divided into contact, close and non-close. Distance, by contrast, is the interval between the muzzle and the target. Range and distance are not the same. At the entrance hole there is often a tissue defect and an abrasion and contamination collar; the exit hole is uneven, without a collar. The examination establishes the type of weapon, the range, the direction of the track and the sequence. The physician must fully document the injury.
